title: Relative estimation: story points and t-shirt sizes
blurb: Explain relative estimation, story points, t-shirt sizing, card-based team estimating and magic estimation, and forecast with velocity.
question: A delivery team is asked how many hours each user story will take. The team coach suggests a different approach recommended by PRINCE2 Agile. What is it, and why does it help?

teach.h: Estimate by comparison, not by the clock
teach.body: PRINCE2 Agile recommends relative rather than actual estimates. Instead of predicting hours, the team sizes each item against other items: is this bigger or smaller than that one? Comparing is quicker than predicting, and a size stays the same even when the team's speed changes. The book also stresses harnessing the whole team, so that everyone contributes and nobody is swayed by others' views.

rows.label: Question asked
values: How big is it next to that?

teach.body: The most common form of relative estimation gives each requirement or user story a points value that means something relative to another story. A 6-point story is roughly twice the size of a 3-point one. Points are not hours. Once the team has delivered a few iterations, its velocity (the average story points delivered per timebox) can be used to forecast, as long as conditions stay the same.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 8.4.3, 12.4.3 and Glossary

teach.h: Story points are sizes, not hours
teach.caption: Each value only has meaning next to the others: 'book an adviser call' is judged bigger than 'compare mortgage deals', not a set number of hours.
T-shirt sizing puts items into a few coarse relative sizes. It suits early estimates when detail is thin. (A typical scale; the exact sizes a team uses can vary.)

items: The product owner explains the story and its acceptance criteria.
Each team member chooses an estimate privately, using pre-numbered cards or paper.
Everyone reveals at the same moment, so nobody is swayed by the others.
Typically, the highest and lowest estimators explain their thinking.
The team re-estimates until it agrees on a size.

teach.body: When there are many items to size early on, for example at the level of the project product, magic estimation helps. It is a quick, collaborative technique for estimating the relative size or complexity of many stories without lengthy discussion. Later, in each team planning workshop, the effort estimation topic gives a shared view of each story's complexity before iteration planning selects stories by priority and estimate.

Team coach Priya Raman runs the mortgage portal team's estimating session. For one story the cards show 3, 3, 5 and 13. The developer who chose 13 explains a hidden integration with the credit check system, and the team settles on 8. Over three iterations the team delivered 18, 22 and 20 points, so its velocity is 20. With 120 points left, it forecasts six more iterations, using its own history rather than another team's.

teach.text: Story points are not hours, and velocity belongs to one team. Forecasting with another team's or one person's rate breaks the empirical approach. Do not confuse magic estimation (fast sizing of many items early on) with card-based estimating of each story, where everyone reveals at once.

items: PRINCE2 Agile prefers relative estimates to actual estimates (8.4.3).
Story points: a value meaningful relative to other stories, not hours.
T-shirt sizing: coarse relative sizes such as small, medium and large.
Simultaneous reveal stops people being swayed; the whole team contributes.
Magic estimation: quick, collaborative sizing of many items in early planning.
Velocity = average story points per timebox; forecast with your own team's figure.

summary: You can now explain why PRINCE2 Agile prefers relative estimates and describe story points, t-shirt sizing, card-based estimating and magic estimation. You can also use a team's own velocity to forecast remaining work.

A.q: What kind of estimates does PRINCE2 Agile recommend for user stories?
options: Relative estimates that compare items with each other
Actual estimates given in hours for each task in turn
Top-down estimates set by the project board per story
Expert estimates made by the project manager for the team
A.why: Book 8.4.3 recommends relative, not actual, estimates, using the whole team so everyone contributes.

whyNot.1: Actual estimates in hours are what relative estimation moves away from.
whyNot.2: The board sets tolerances; it does not size individual stories.
whyNot.3: Estimates should harness the whole team, not rely on one person.

A.q: A team gives each user story a points value that means something relative to other stories. What is this technique?
A.why: Story points are the most common form of relative estimation: a points value meaningful relative to another story (8.4.3).

whyNot.0: T-shirt sizing uses coarse sizes such as small, medium and large rather than points.
whyNot.2: Magic estimation is a fast way to size many items at once in early planning; giving each story a relative points value is the story points technique.
whyNot.3: Velocity tracking measures points delivered per timebox; it does not assign values to stories.

A.q: When a team estimates with pre-numbered cards, why does everyone reveal their estimate at the same time?
options: So the project manager can approve the total
So each estimate can be converted to hours
So the most senior developer sets the baseline
So that nobody is swayed by others' estimates
A.why: Simultaneous reveal lets each member contribute an independent view without being swayed by others (8.4.3).

whyNot.0: Story estimates are a team matter; the project manager does not approve them.
whyNot.1: Relative estimates are deliberately not converted into hours.
whyNot.2: Letting one senior voice set the figure is exactly what the simultaneous reveal avoids.

B.q: Which technique suits early planning, such as at project product level, to size many stories quickly without lengthy discussion?
B.why: Magic estimation is a quick, collaborative technique used in early planning to estimate the relative size of many items without lengthy discussion (8.4.3).

whyNot.0: Card-based estimating discusses each story in turn, which is slower for a large list.
whyNot.1: A product breakdown structure describes products and their components; it does not size them.
whyNot.3: A cumulative flow diagram tracks work in each workflow state; it is a progress technique.

B.q: A team estimates user stories by placing them in clothing-style sizes such as small, medium and large. What is this?
B.why: T-shirt sizing is a relative estimation technique named in the syllabus alongside story points (8.4.3).

whyNot.0: MoSCoW sets priority (Must, Should, Could, Won't), not size.
whyNot.1: Story mapping orders user activities and breaks them into stories.
whyNot.2: Delegation poker defines how decisions are delegated in a team.

B.q:
Which two statements about relative estimation are correct?
1. Story points express size relative to other stories.
2. Story points are a direct count of the hours a story will take.
3. The whole team contributes so that no single view dominates.
4. The project board sets the estimate for each story.
B.why: Story points are relative values (1), and PRINCE2 Agile harnesses the whole team so nobody is swayed by others (3) (8.4.3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: points are relative sizes, not hours.
whyNot.2: Both 2 and 4 are wrong: points are not hours and the board does not estimate stories.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: the delivery team estimates, not the board.

C.q: A team delivered 18, 22 and 20 story points in its last three iterations and has 120 points left. Using its velocity, how many more iterations should it forecast?
C.why: Velocity is the average: (18 + 22 + 20) / 3 = 20 points per iteration. 120 / 20 = 6 iterations.

whyNot.0: Five would need a velocity of 24, higher than the team has achieved.
whyNot.2: Seven assumes about 17 points per iteration, below the team's average of 20.
whyNot.3: Eight assumes 15 points per iteration, below every recent result.

C.q: A newly formed team must forecast its first release. Which approach does PRINCE2 Agile favour?
options: Start work and measure the team's own rate
Use a similar team's velocity from last year
Ask the most senior developer for a figure
Convert story points to hours at a set rate
C.why: PRINCE2 Agile favours empiricism: start work, measure how much gets done (calibration) and forecast from your own team's velocity (8.3).

whyNot.1: Another team's velocity is not a reliable basis; use your own team's.
whyNot.2: One person's figure is not empirical and does not harness the whole team.
whyNot.3: Points are relative sizes; converting them to hours defeats relative estimation.

C.q: In the team planning workshop, which topic gives a shared view of each story's complexity, and which topic then selects stories for the iteration?
C.why: Effort estimation builds a shared view of complexity and effort; iteration planning then selects stories by priority and estimate into a realistic team plan (Table 13.13).

whyNot.1: Backlog refinement prioritizes the backlog and user story refinement sharpens acceptance criteria; neither sizes nor selects stories.
whyNot.3: User story refinement clarifies acceptance criteria; it does not build the shared view of effort.

reteach.title: Weigh it against something you know
reteach.question: If you had to guess a suitcase's weight, would you rather name a figure in kilograms or say whether it is heavier than the one beside it?

blocks.body: People are better at saying 'this is about twice that one' than at naming an exact figure. Relative estimation uses that: pick a story the team knows, call it 3 points or a Medium, and size everything else against it. The team then measures how many points it really finishes per iteration, and that velocity turns sizes into a forecast.

blocks.text: A forecast is only as good as its velocity: use your own team's measured rate, not a guess or another team's figure.

explain.body: PRINCE2 Agile estimates by comparing items with other items rather than predicting hours, and it involves the whole team so nobody is swayed.

test.q: What does a relative estimate compare an item with?
test.why: Relative estimation sizes an item against other items (8.4.3).

whyNot.1: Comparing with available hours is an actual (time-based) estimate.
whyNot.2: The budget is a cost constraint, not the reference for sizing.
whyNot.3: Tolerances limit deviation; they are not a sizing reference.

explain.body: Story points give each story a value relative to others. Velocity is the average story points a team delivers per timebox, used to forecast empirically while conditions stay the same.

options: The number of stories in the product backlog
The average story points delivered per timebox
The time one story takes from start to done
The hours each developer works per iteration
test.why: Velocity is the average rate of story points delivered per timebox for one or more teams (Glossary, 12.4.3).

whyNot.0: Backlog size is the work remaining, not a rate of delivery.
whyNot.2: The time one item takes is closer to Kanban cycle time, not velocity.
whyNot.3: Velocity measures points delivered, not hours worked.

explain.body: T-shirt sizing groups items into coarse relative sizes. Card-based estimating has each member pick a value privately and reveal it at the same time, then discuss differences.

test.q: Which is an example of t-shirt sizing?
options: Marking a story as a Must have
test.why: T-shirt sizing places a story in a relative size bucket such as Medium.

whyNot.0: A points value is story point estimation.
whyNot.1: Must have is a MoSCoW priority, not a size.
whyNot.3: Hours are an actual estimate, not a relative one.

explain.body: Magic estimation is a quick, collaborative technique for sizing many items in early planning, such as at project product level, without long discussion of each one.

test.q: Magic estimation is BEST described as:
options: a statistical forecast built by project support
a detailed task breakdown for one iteration
a risk score for each story in the backlog
a quick, collaborative way to size many items
test.why: Magic estimation is a quick, collaborative way to estimate the relative size of many items without lengthy discussion (8.4.3).

whyNot.0: It is done by the team together, not built as a statistical model by project support.
whyNot.1: Task breakdown for one iteration is the team plan.
whyNot.2: Risk levels are tracked per risk on the cumulative risk burn-down chart, a risk technique; magic estimation sizes work items.
